problem:
Complete the arguments in the reasoning below to find the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{t/4}.$First, we apply the definition of the Laplace transform:

$$
L{f(t)}=F(s)={{field-1}}
$$

We now examine the convergence of $F(s)$ for different values of $s:$

$\,$ For {{field-2}}
the integral is convergent.

$\,$ For {{field-3}}
the integral is divergent.

Evaluating our integral in the convergent case, we have

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(1/4-s)t}\,\text{d}t={{field-4}}.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that $L{{e}^{t/4}}=\frac{4}{4s-1},$ 
defined for
{{field-5}}.
worked_solution:
For a function $f(t)$ defined on $[0,\infty ),$ the Laplace transform of $f,$ denoted $L{f(t)}$ or $F(s),$ is a function of the variable $s$ defined as

$$
F(s)=L{f(t)}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

provided that this integral exists and is finite. 

For the function $f(t)={e}^{t/4},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{t/4}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st+t/4}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(1/4-s)t}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We calculate our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(1/4-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(1/4-s)t}\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

To evaluate the last integral, we must consider whether $s\ne \frac{1}{4}$ or $s=\frac{1}{4}.$

- If $s\ne \frac{1}{4},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(1/4-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{(\frac{1}{1/4-s}{e}^{(1/4-s)t})|}_{0}^{a} \\  & =\frac{1}{1/4-s}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(1/4-s)a}-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{s-1/4}(1-{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(1/4-s)a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{s-1/4}-\frac{1}{s-1/4}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(1/4-s)a}\end{aligned}
$$

Let's evaluate the limit. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(1/4-s)a}={\begin{aligned}0,\, & s>\frac{1}{4}, \\ \infty ,\, & s<\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

- If $s=\frac{1}{4},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(\frac{1}{4}) & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(1/4-1/4)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{0t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }t\,{|}_{0}^{a} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }(a-0) \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }a \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore:

- For $s>\frac{1}{4}$ the integral is convergent.

- For $s\le \frac{1}{4}$ the integral is divergent.

Evaluating for $s>\frac{1}{4},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =\frac{1}{s-1/4}-\frac{1}{s-1/4}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(1/4-s)a} \\  & =\frac{1}{s-1/4}-\frac{1}{s-1/4}\cdot 0 \\  & =\frac{1}{s-1/4} \\  & =\frac{4}{4s-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{t/4}$ is $F(s)=\frac{4}{4s-1},$ defined for $s>\frac{1}{4}.$
